1170.title: Block close: reason and faith
1170.hook: Maimonides shows reason can serve faith
1170.howItsDone: Jews study Maimonides' code and his Guide in yeshivas, universities and study groups, and his principles of faith appear in prayer books in the hymn Yigdal and the Ani Ma'amin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thought and deed: a law code that starts with knowing God, and a philosophy that ends in kindness. Your line: thought and deed. Today, the block closes.

An epitaph that says none like Moses. A commentary on the Mishnah. A list of principles of faith. Chapters on the health of the soul, and a middle way. A code of law in clear Hebrew. The rungs of giving. A path of return. A picture of the messianic age. A guide for the perplexed, with silence as praise. Then the arguments, the son, the honest reading, the grave by the lake. One question sits underneath it all: can a mind that asks hard questions still stand before God?
screen: `NONE LIKE MOSES.` → `ONE MAN, MANY BOOKS.` → `ONE QUESTION UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Block close: reason and faith. First, reason is part of obeying. The Torah says the nations will hear these laws and call Israel "a wise and understanding people." Maimonides leans on that verse in the Guide: if outsiders can see the wisdom, the commandments must have reasons a mind can look for. Thinking isn't a threat to the law. It's one way of honoring it. Second, reason clears the way. You saw him do it with God's hand and God's eye: figures of speech, he said, not a body. And with praise: sometimes the truest thing a mind can offer is silence. Reason sweeps away wrong pictures so a truer reverence has room. Third, reason knows its edge. About the messianic age he said nobody will know how until it happens. About God he said we know better what God is not. Fourth, reason ends in love and in deed. His code says a person who looks at the wonders of creation is moved to love and to awe, and his Guide ends with kindness, justice and righteousness. For Maimonides, thinking isn't the opposite of faith. It's one of the ways faith is served. Not everyone agreed, then or now: you met the Rabad's sharp notes, and the Ramban's other way, toward a hidden layer in the Torah. Tomorrow a new block begins with that hidden layer: the tradition called Kabbalah, a different road into the same Torah.
screen: `A WISE AND UNDERSTANDING PEOPLE.` · `REASON CLEARS THE WAY.` · `REASON KNOWS ITS EDGE.` · `REASON ENDS IN LOVE AND DEED.` · then, large: `REASON SERVES FAITH.`

segments.voice: Pick one question you've been carrying, about faith, a choice or a person, and think it through slowly, the way Maimonides liked: what do I actually know, and what am I only picturing? When you reach the edge of what you can know, stop there, and let the rest be quiet.
Block close. This stretch with Maimonides ends here: reason that searches, clears away wrong pictures, knows its edge, and leads to love and deed. Today's word.
Your line: reason serves faith. A careful mind can tell where its knowing stops. I'll be here tomorrow.

1171.title: Received tradition
1171.hook: Kabbalah means "receiving", the name for Jewish mystical tradition
1171.howItsDone: Jews welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening with the Kabbalat Shabbat service, and those who study Kabbalah read its texts, such as the Zohar, often in study groups or with a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maimonides block closed: reason that searches, knows its edge, and ends in love and deed. Your line: reason serves faith. Today, a new road begins.

Buy a coffee in Tel Aviv and ask for a receipt, and the Hebrew word you'll hear is kabbalah. The same word names something that sounds nothing like a coffee shop: the Jewish mystical tradition, with its talk of God's hidden life and the secret depths of the Torah. One word for a slip of paper and a doorway into mystery. And it says something about where this tradition thinks its wisdom comes from.
screen: `A RECEIPT FOR A COFFEE.` → `A MYSTICAL TRADITION.` → `ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Kabbalah. First, the root. Kabbalah comes from a Hebrew root meaning to receive. A receipt is what you receive. It's the same root in the opening line of Pirkei Avot: Moses received the Torah from Sinai and handed it on to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, and onward, teacher to student. Kabbalah, at its simplest, is what has been received. Second, receiving in daily life. On Friday evening, synagogues pray a service called Kabbalat Shabbat, receiving the Sabbath, welcoming it in like a guest at the door. So the word lives in ordinary Jewish life before it ever means mysticism. Third, the name for a tradition. Over time, Kabbalah became the name for a body of Jewish mystical teaching: how God, who is beyond all knowing, is still revealed in the world, and the hidden layers of meaning in the letters of the Torah. You met a hint of it when the Ramban spoke of meanings known by the way of truth. Among its books is the Zohar, the radiance, which this block will come to. Fourth, received, not invented. The mystics didn't call their teaching discovery or innovation. They called it what was received, something handed down. Whatever a reader concludes about its history, the name says how its teachers understood themselves: as links in a chain. And they read old texts closely, like Isaiah's vision of the seraphim calling out, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts."
screen: `A ROOT THAT MEANS TO RECEIVE.` · `KABBALAT SHABBAT: RECEIVING THE SABBATH.` · `A NAME FOR JEWISH MYSTICISM.` · `RECEIVED, NOT INVENTED.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.`

1172.title: Enter carefully
1172.hook: traditionally for the mature and learned; today many study it with a teacher
1172.howItsDone: Jewish mystical texts have traditionally been studied by people already grounded in Torah and Talmud; today they are also taught in classes and study circles, usually with a teacher guiding the reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabbalah: a word that means receiving, and the name of Jewish mystical tradition. Your line: the received. Today, the warning at its door.

There's a rule in the Mishnah that reads like a sign on a door. Some subjects, it says, are not to be taught in a crowd. The account of creation, not to two at once. The chariot that Ezekiel saw, not even to one, unless that one is already wise and understands on their own. The rest of the Torah carries no such sign. Tradition kept the mystical teachings for people who were mature and already learned. Today, people study them in classes and books, often with a teacher beside them.
screen: `A RULE LIKE A SIGN ON A DOOR.` → `NOT TO TWO. NOT EVEN TO ONE.` → `A NARROW DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Enter carefully. The Talmud tells a short, strange story about why. Four sages, it says, entered the pardes, the orchard; some readers hear it as the hidden depths of the Torah. Ben Azzai looked, and died. Ben Zoma looked, and was harmed. Elisha ben Abuyah, whom the Talmud calls Acher, the other one, cut down the shoots, which readers take to mean he left the path. Only Rabbi Akiva, the story says, entered in peace and went out in peace. First, the orchard is real enough to hurt. The story doesn't say mystical study is bad. It says it's strong, and strength needs care. Second, look at who walks out whole. The story doesn't say why it was Akiva. Some readers point to what else the Talmud tells of him: a teacher of the law, surrounded by students, steeped in the plain sense of the text. On that reading, the ground you stand on before you go in counts for a great deal. Third, the door isn't locked forever. The same tradition that warns at the doorway also kept the teachings, copied them and handed them down. Caution was a way of protecting them, not burying them. Fourth, the teacher. The Mishnah's picture is a sage beside one student, not a stranger with a book: someone who has been in the orchard and can say, slow down, look here, not yet. So entering carefully is less about fear than about humility: knowing you're a guest in a very old garden.
screen: `FOUR ENTERED THE ORCHARD.` · `THE ORCHARD IS STRONG.` · `AKIVA, WHO KNEW THE GROUND.` · `A TEACHER BESIDE YOU.` · then, large: `IN PEACE, AND OUT IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want to understand but don't yet, a text, a skill, a person, a question about God, and say to yourself quietly: I don't know this yet. Notice how it feels to stand at the door instead of pushing through it. Then hold the name of one person who could walk you in, a teacher, a friend, or someone who writes carefully.

1173.title: The Book of Creation
1173.hook: an ancient short book on creation through letters and numbers
1173.howItsDone: Sefer Yetzirah is studied as a foundational text of Kabbalah, usually alongside its commentaries, and some teachers begin by having students learn to look closely at the Hebrew letters themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four sages walked into the orchard, and only Akiva walked out in peace. Your line: enter carefully. Today, a small, strange book about letters.

On the Torah's first page, the world gets made without hands. Not with tools. God speaks. "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." Over and over on that page: God said, and it was so. Words, and words are made of letters. So a question follows, if you sit with that page long enough. What are the letters doing? Are they just how the story was written down, or part of how it happened? A small, strange book takes that question all the way.
screen: `GOD SAID, AND IT WAS SO.` → `WORDS ARE MADE OF LETTERS.` → `WHAT ARE THE LETTERS DOING?`

segments.voice: Sefer Yetzirah. The Book of Creation, or the Book of Formation. It's short, and it reads less like a story than a riddle. First, its opening. The world was created, it says, through paths of wisdom, and it names what those paths are made of: ten sefirot, and the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Ten and twenty-two; the book itself counts them. You'll meet that word, sefirot, again in a few days, grown much larger. Second, what it does with the letters. The book describes them being engraved, carved, weighed, combined and turned around, one with another, and says that with them everything that is formed was formed. Letters as building blocks, not just labels. Third, its company. The Talmud has its own small story in this direction: Bezalel, who built the tabernacle in the desert, knew how to join the letters by which heaven and earth were created. A craftsman whose real skill was the alphabet. Fourth, the name tradition puts on it. Some versions of the book end with Abraham, and tradition ties the book to him. Scholars ask other questions about its origins, and the book itself doesn't settle them. What it gives you instead is a way of looking: if the world was spoken, then every letter on the page has a little of the beginning in it. Kabbalists would build a great deal on this short book.
screen: `PATHS OF WISDOM.` · `LETTERS ENGRAVED, WEIGHED, COMBINED.` · `BEZALEL KNEW THE LETTERS.` · `A BOOK TIED TO ABRAHAM.` · then, large: `LETTERS CREATE.`

segments.voice: If you have a prayer book, a Torah, or a picture of the Hebrew alphabet on your phone, open it; you don't need to read Hebrew, because you're looking, not reading. Rest your eyes on one letter and notice its shape, the open side, the closed side, the little crown or hook at its top, then move slowly to the next. Let each letter be a shape before it's a sound, and a sound before it's a word.
Sefer Yetzirah. The Book of Creation: a short, riddle-like book that describes the world formed through paths of wisdom, the sefirot and the Hebrew letters. Today's word.
Your line: letters create. On the Torah's first page, speaking was making. See you tomorrow.

1174.title: Without end
1174.hook: God as the Infinite, beyond any description
1174.howItsDone: In Kabbalah, Ein Sof is the term for God beyond all description; students usually meet it at the start of an introduction to the sefirot, as the one source from which everything else unfolds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sefer Yetzirah, where letters are engraved, weighed and combined to form the world. Your line: letters create. Today, a name that refuses every line.

How do you draw something with no edges? Every drawing starts with a line, and a line is a boundary: this is inside, that is outside. A word works the same way. Call something kind, and you've drawn a line around it, kind and not cruel. Now try it with God. Every word you reach for draws a line. Wise. Strong. Near. Each one is true in its way, and each one is too small. Jewish mystics gave that problem a name, a name that is really a refusal to draw any line at all.
screen: `EVERY DRAWING STARTS WITH A LINE.` → `EVERY WORD DRAWS A BOUNDARY.` → `EACH ONE IS TOO SMALL.`

segments.voice: Ein Sof. In Hebrew, ein means there is no, and sof means end. Without end. Kabbalists use it for God as God is in God's own self, before and beyond any way of being known. First, it's hardly a name. A name usually tells you what something is. This one tells you only what it is not: not ending, not bounded, not measured. After weeks with Maimonides, you'll hear a cousin of his teaching, that we speak more truly of God by saying what God is not. The kabbalists take that silence and give it a title. Second, the Psalms point the same way. The psalmist praises God, then admits that God's greatness is beyond searching out. Praise, and then the edge of what praise can do. Third, Ein Sof is not a second God hiding behind the first. Kabbalists insist that God is one. Ein Sof is the one God from the side that can't be spoken of: not a different being, but the same One, seen from where every word runs out. Fourth, the turn. If God is without end, beyond every description, how does God touch a world with edges, a world of kitchens and buses and birthdays? That question drives the whole system ahead, and the mystics answer it with lights. For today, just stand where they stood, at the edge of the drawing, looking at the space with no line around it.
screen: `THERE IS NO END.` · `A NAME THAT SAYS WHAT GOD IS NOT.` · `NOT A SECOND GOD.` · `HOW DOES THE ENDLESS TOUCH THE WORLD?` · then, large: `WITHOUT END.`

segments.voice: Go to a window or step outside if you can, or close your eyes and remember the widest sky you've ever seen, and let your eyes rise past the roofs and wires and trees to where there's nothing to rest on. When your gaze wants an edge, a cloud, a bird, let it keep going instead. If you pray, you can simply be quiet before the One without end.
Ein Sof. Without end: the kabbalists' way of speaking of God as God is in God's self, beyond every name and description. Today's word.
Your line: without end. Every word for God draws a line; this name refuses to. That's today, done.

1175.title: Ten lights
1175.hook: ten emanations through which the Infinite relates to the world
1175.howItsDone: Students of Kabbalah learn the ten sefirot by name and order, often drawn as a diagram, and Hasidic teaching applies them to a person's own character and inner life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ein Sof: God without end, beyond every description, and a question left hanging: how does the endless touch a world with edges? Your line: without end. Today, the mystics' answer.

"Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty." King David says it in the book of Chronicles, blessing God in front of the whole assembly. It sounds like one long sweep of praise. But slow down and count the nouns. In Hebrew each one is its own word, and Jewish mystics read them as more than praise. To them it was a list: names of the ways the one God shows up in the world. That list has a name of its own.
screen: `THINE, O LORD, IS THE GREATNESS.` → `COUNT THE NOUNS.` → `NOT JUST PRAISE. A LIST.`

segments.voice: Sefirot. You met the word two days ago in Sefer Yetzirah. In Kabbalah it grows into a whole map: ten lights, or ten emanations, through which Ein Sof, God without end, relates to the world. First, the number. Sefer Yetzirah insists on it: ten, and not nine; ten, and not eleven. A shape with a definite count. Second, the names. One common order runs: Keter, crown. Chochmah, wisdom. Binah, understanding. Chesed, love. Gevurah, strength. Tiferet, beauty. Netzach, endurance. Hod, splendor. Yesod, foundation. And Malchut, kingship. Listen for David's verse inside it: gevurah, tiferet, netzach, hod. Kabbalists heard those sefirot in that very line. Third, the warning. Ten lights does not mean ten gods. Sefer Yetzirah says their end is bound up in their beginning, like a flame tied to a coal. One fire, many tongues of flame. Kabbalists say again and again that God is one, and the sefirot are how that one God is turned toward us. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary afternoon. The sefirot are also qualities a person has: love, restraint, balance, steadiness, the ability to bring something into the world. Kabbalists read the human being as built in the same pattern, so the map of how God meets the world doubles as a map of a life.
screen: `TEN, AND NOT NINE.` · `CROWN DOWN TO KINGSHIP.` · `A FLAME TIED TO A COAL.` · `A MAP OF A LIFE, TOO.` · then, large: `TEN LIGHTS.`

segments.voice: On each slow breath, say one name quietly with its meaning, from the top down: Keter, crown; Chochmah, wisdom; Binah, understanding; Chesed, love; Gevurah, strength; Tiferet, beauty; Netzach, endurance; Hod, splendor; Yesod, foundation; Malchut, kingship. Don't worry about getting the order perfect. Let one name catch on something in your own life, and stay with that one.
Sefirot. The ten lights, or emanations, through which, in Kabbalah, the one God without end relates to the world, from crown to kingship. Today's word.
Your line: ten lights. Ten of them, and still one fire with many tongues of flame. Until tomorrow.

1176.title: Crown, wisdom, understanding
1176.hook: Keter, Chochmah, Binah: will, the flash of an idea, and its unfolding
1176.howItsDone: In Kabbalah, Keter, Chochmah and Binah are taught as the highest sefirot; Chabad Hasidism takes its name from Chochmah, Binah and Da'at, and its teaching applies them to how a person thinks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sefirot: ten lights from crown down to kingship, one fire with many tongues of flame. Your line: ten lights. Today, the top three.

In the shower, on a walk, halfway through washing a pan: the idea arrives. All at once, whole, before you have words for it. Then comes the long part. You sit down and work it out, piece by piece, until the flash becomes a plan someone else could follow. And underneath both, before either, there was something quieter: the wanting to solve it in the first place. Kabbalists saw those three moments at the very top of the ten lights.
screen: `THE IDEA ARRIVES, WHOLE.` → `THEN THE LONG WORKING OUT.` → `BEFORE BOTH, YOU WANTED IT.`

segments.voice: Keter, Chochmah, Binah: crown, wisdom, understanding. First, the crown. A crown sits above the head, not inside it. Kabbalists place Keter above thought and link it to will, the deep wanting that comes before any idea. Some teachers say so little can be said of it that it borders on Ein Sof itself. Second, wisdom, Chochmah: the flash, a point of light before it has length or width. The book of Job asks, "But where shall wisdom be found?" In Hebrew the word for where can also be read as from nothing, and kabbalists heard Job saying that wisdom comes from nothing: out of the hidden crown, a sudden point. Third, understanding, Binah: the unfolding. Binah takes the point and gives it room, corridors and details, the way a seed becomes a plant. Kabbalists picture the two as a pair, a father and a mother. The flash needs the unfolding, or it stays a spark. The unfolding needs the flash, or it has nothing to build. Fourth, where the three words meet. When the Torah introduces Bezalel, the craftsman you met joining letters, God fills him "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge." In Hebrew: chochmah, binah, da'at, the three words one Hasidic school, Chabad, took as its name. Look back across this week: reason serving faith, the received tradition, the careful doorway, the letters, the One without end, the ten lights, and now the top three. A week spent climbing to the crown.
screen: `CROWN: THE WILL ABOVE THOUGHT.` · `WISDOM: THE FLASH FROM NOTHING.` · `UNDERSTANDING: THE UNFOLDING.` · `WISDOM, UNDERSTANDING, KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `THE FLASH AND THE UNFOLDING.`

segments.voice: Hold one small, real question in front of you, what to cook tonight or how to begin a task, and wait for an answer the way you'd wait for a bird to land. When something arrives, notice the moment before it had words, then let it unfold slowly into one plain sentence. If nothing comes, notice the wanting underneath, and rest there.
Crown. Keter, the top of the ten lights: the will that sits above thought, before wisdom flashes and understanding unfolds. Today's word.
Your line: the flash and the unfolding. And before both, the wanting. Back tomorrow, same hill.
